stories.title_en: Denmark Data Breach Exposes 8.8M People's Personal Data

comments.author: aiiotnoodle
comments.text:
I'm seriously at a point where I'm opposed to talking to my doctor because the information may be digitally recorded and leaked, going on a flight because my passport may be used to aqquire a loan by cybercriminals, comparing car insurance because my phone will be called by robocallers selling me things or verifying my ID with websites because it might be used to associate my information with whatever else I do online.
I don't think, for a vast majority of cases, these companies I'm forced to interact with can be trusted with my data and it's having a real world negative impact. Even with the best intentions the information is somehow valuable to steal and I'm baffled how it's not secure.
There should be some consequences for companies asking for things like SSN/National Insurance numbers on job adverts or retaining drivers licence photos after test driving a car, they just don't need the data anymore.

comments.author: Jackson__
comments.text:
I've just tested Strata on a simple 50 image vision benchmark. The task is to output the exact coordinates of a requested object. The result via Strata had a median error distance of 154.8 pixels, avg of 168.8. Running the exact same GGUF and vision adapter weights on llama.cpp gives me a median error of 46.5, avg 81.4.
To put that into perspective, here are some more numbers from other models via llama.cpp:
Median/Average
Qwen 3.5 9B BF16: 46.5 / 193.3
Qwen 3.6 35B Q4 K XL: 38.4 / 76.4
Qwen 3.5 122B Q3 K M: 32.9 / 68.6
The difference in vision performance is as large as the jump from a 9B model to a 35B model. All tests were performed at temp=0.
I have done no further testing, as these results line up perfectly with my expectations.

comments.author: noduerme
comments.text:
The game state being a SQL table just kinda triggered a memory of a year of optimization for me. One thing I'm still unsure of being a good decision or a bad one, when I wrote my casino in 2010, was having every remote call update game states on SQL tables that were used as the source of truth. With multiple players you can imagine that there would sometimes be issues. Some of the deadlock problems early on were horrific; scaling was a nightmare. But everything was atomic. No risk of lost data beyond one turn not reaching the server or deadlocking, nothing like a huge nodejs process choking on everyone's calls at the same time, or losing its memory. You always had
state
.
Looking back it seems like not a terrible design pattern for multiplayer turn-based games, if you can work out the kinks. Atomicity guarantees at least that there
is
a  consistent state that won't get lost.  Doing that read/write loop for an action game? Pure folly, but it's pretty funny to me.

These games are often playable for free, because they're released for competitions that stipulate the submission must be free.

The key properties for using such models for conditional-branching decisions in agentic stacks (and related) is that they should be well-calibrated (under the definition chosen for the task) and informative (e.g., always predicting the mean might be "well-calibrated" in a theoretical sense for some chosen quantities of interest, but isn't particularly useful in practice).
The tricky thing with the neural networks is that the output logits are in effect a highly lossy compression of the epistemic (reducible) uncertainty, so even if the target calibration quantity is well-specified, it can be difficult to obtain in practice. A side-effect of this is that estimates in the high probability regions are not particularly stable under even modest co-variate shifts, which is a real problem if the estimates are being used for decision-making in a multi-step search graph that can lead to branches that are unlike what the model/estimator saw at training/calibration (if not altogether out-of-distribution). stories.title_en: Demystifying Tufte's data-ink ratio

comments.author: gjm11
comments.text:
I think the idea that a bar chart is usually improved by narrowing its bars while keeping them in the same positions is pretty silly. Yes, the article does say that one can take it too far, but I think that's the wrong framing. It's not that
using less ink is good, but sometimes if you take that too far then it competes with visual clarity
. Visual clarity is always the goal; sometimes clearer designs have more non-data ink, sometimes less; many designs are too busy so "less non-data ink" is usually good, but not always.
Tufte's "data-ink ratio" is a pretty good heuristic, but e.g. it would probably become a better match for actual visual clarity if what you counted wasn't "amount of ink" but something that measures
spatial change
in ink. It's the transitions that feel like noise, much more than patches of constant colour. But "data-ink ratio" is easier to say and easier to read than "ratio of integral of norm of gradient of colour".
Also, I think this sort of graph is better with very light gridlines than with no gridlines, though I think Tufte would disagree.
Also also, in Tufte's book, immediately before the section about "data-ink" there is an copy of a graph drawn by Playfair

comments.author: BrenBarn
comments.text:
I remember getting Tufte's book ("The Visual Display of Quantitative Information") and being really excited because I'd heard all these great things about it, and then being disappointed because it had no real justification for its claims.  The "data ink" thing is a typical example.  I'm willing to accept the general concept that many graphs are too cluttered.  But there's no particular reason to suppose that quantifying the proportion of "data ink" and trying to optimize it is the best way to handle that.  A lot of the book is just taking subjective aesthetic judgements and trying to frame them as some kind of objective truth.
If we really wanted reliable guidelines on how to format graphs, we would want to ground them in psychological research that actually demonstrates that, for instance, some versions result in better understanding or recall of certain information.  But as far as I can see Tufte's book makes no attempt to do this.  (Perhaps he or those who built on his works did it later on?)

When I read the headline, I thought the article was about fans (and the attached lights) that mysteriously turn themselves on without the owner doing anything.
This happened to us, and the people we bought the house from had actually bought (but not installed) a new controller.  Turned out the problem wasn't the controller at all.  Rather, all the houses on the street had been built at the same time by the same company, and most (maybe all) had ceiling fans that came with a remote.  Inside the remote and inside the fan was a DIP-switch consisting of four switches, each switch labeled with a 0 and a 1 depending on which way you pushed it.  And all probably came from the factory with a 0000 setting.
You guessed it: while ordinarily the controller had a limited range, sometimes (windows open? controller pointed in a certain direction? I don't know) one neighbor's controller would activate someone else's fan.  The solution was of course simple: set the DIP switch in our fan and controller to some other setting, like 0101.  Since I did that, the poltergeist has been unable to operate our ceiling fans.

comments.text:
The problem isn't that you can't use AI to uplevel your creativity. It's that doing it slows you down, so you end up at a marked disadvantage, because others who just prompt "hey Claude, make me X" will produce 100 good enough slop-pieces in the time it takes you to finish one.
For the vast majority of paying customers or social media appreciators, that low-effort slop is sufficient. It's cheap, fast, and gets better with every passing month. So if your overriding goal is to
scale
to win in that marketplace, then you can only scale by giving up on quality and artistry. It's a race to the bottom.
I think the only way to win is to push back on the notion that you need to work on superhuman scale in the first place. You can differentiate yourself from AI by asserting you're human and that there's inherent value in human art. You'll find some customers willing to pay extra for that, just like some hire a woodworker instead of buying at Ikea. But it's going to be a tough market for artisans because fewer and fewer people are
forced
to buy the fruits of your intellectual labor.
In software engineering specifically, we gleefully decided that speed and cost are the only thing that matters

comments.author: atombender
comments.text:
Blindsight is fantastic. The sequel, Echopraxia, is also excellent; it is very different, and I expect many people were disappointed that it wasn't just more of the same.
Also a big shout out to his less well-known novel, The Freeze Frame Revolution. It's about the crew of a "stargate"-seeding spaceship trying to stop the ship's AI, but being hampered by the fact that the AI is both near-omniscient and that they only work in short shifts before being put back in hibernation. He also wrote a handful of short stories set before and after the novel.
There's something very refreshingly direct, unvarnished, no-nonsense, and clear-eyed (some would say cynical) about Watts' style of writing. His prose tends to be tough (quite like early Gibson's noir style, with the punk attitude intact), but also beautifully cinematic. The only other write that I think comes close, aside from Gibson, is Dan Simmons with his Hyperion Cantos, but he's not nearly as darkly cynical.
